<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, here is a detailed explanation of how to create an accurate system design diagram for mcp-golang:

1. Project Type and Purpose:
   • mcp-golang is an unofficial Go implementation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Its purpose is to allow developers to rapidly write both servers and clients that implement MCP using Go. The library’s modular design covers tool, prompt, and resource calls, and supports multiple transports (e.g., stdio, HTTP, Gin, SSE).
   • The README emphasizes type safety, low boilerplate integration, and modularity. These highlights suggest that the design should separate concerns between protocol handling, transport mechanisms, and the server/client logic.

2. Analyzing the File Structure:
   • Top-Level Files: There are files like client.go, server.go, content_api.go, and various API definitions (e.g., tool_api.go, prompt_api.go, resource_api.go) which indicate that the core functionality is split between client functionality and server endpoints.
   • Directories:
     – docs: Contains architecture documentation (docs/architecture.mdx) and guides. This is a useful reference for the diagram’s context.
     – examples: Provides practical use cases (server, client, and several transport examples) that illustrate how the system functions in different scenarios.
     – internal: Contains subdirectories such as protocol, schema, datastructures, and testing utilities. These implement the internal mechanics of protocol processing, message encoding/decoding, schema generation, and testing patterns.
     – transport: Contains implementations for different transports (e.g., stdio, HTTP, Gin, SSE). This clearly indicates that the design separates transport layer logic from core protocol and business logic.
     – Other files like go.mod, go.sum, and .github workflows indicate CI/CD integration and dependency management but are less central to the architectural diagram.

3. Main Components for the Diagram:
   a. Core Components:
      • Server/Client Core: Represented by files such as server.go, client.go, tool_api.go, prompt_api.go, and resource_api.go. These handle the high-level registration and invocation of tools, prompts, and resources.
      • Protocol: The “internal/protocol” directory and associated tests handle encoding/decoding and other protocol-level concerns.
      • Schema Generation: In internal/schema, which generates and manages the automatic generation of JSON schemas from Go structs.
      • Utilities & Datastructures: In internal/datastructures and internal/testingutils, which support the core functionalities.
   b. Transport Layer:
      • Multiple implementations (stdio, HTTP, Gin, SSE) are provided in the “transport” directory. This layer abstracts the communication protocol between the server and the client.
   c. External Interactions:
      • Tools, Prompts, and Resources: These are the registered endpoints that the server will expose, and which the client can call.
      • Custom Transports: The design allows for plugging in custom transports, making the architecture extensible.
      • Integration with third-party tools such as Claude (as indicated by the dedicated instructions in the README).

4. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The server component accepts registrations for tools, prompts, and resources. It then uses the defined protocol to generate endpoints automatically.
   • The transport layer acts as an abstraction between the server/client core and the underlying communication mechanism. Different transports provide either bidirectional (stdio, SSE) or stateless (HTTP, Gin) communications.
   • Example directories show how clients can invoke server methods and use different transports to communicate.

5. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity: The library has a clear separation between the transport, protocol, and business logic layers.
   • Layered Architecture: The design clearly distinguishes between lower-level utilities (protocol handling, schema generation), transport implementations, and high-level server/client APIs.
   • Extensibility: Custom transports can be plugged in, suggesting an interface-based design that decouples communication details from core logic.

6. Specific Guidelines for Diagram Construction:
   • Begin by drawing three main sections (or layers):
     1. Core Server/Client Logic: Include components for tool, prompt, and resource API handling.
     2. Protocol and Schema: Add a block for internal protocol processing and schema generation.
     3. Transport Layer: Represent the various transport implementations (stdio, HTTP, Gin, SSE). Use separate boxes or icons for each transport mechanism.
   • From the Core Server/Client block, draw directional arrows to the protocol block (indicating that outgoing requests are encoded/decoded via the protocol) and vice versa.
   • Next, from the protocol layer, indicate communication with the appropriate transport implementations. Label arrows with data flow (e.g., “message encoding”, “endpoint registration”, “tool invocation”).
   • Include an external “Client” block (or boxes representing different clients) that connects via the transport layer to the server.
   • Optionally, illustrate examples of how external users invoke the tools/prompts and how custom transports can be plugged in.

7. Diagram Elements to Include:
   • Clear Labels: Ensure that each component such as “Server (Tool/Prompt/Resource API)”, “Protocol Handler”, “Schema Generator”, and “Transport Implementations (stdio, HTTP, Gin, SSE)” is clearly labeled.
   • Directional Arrows: Use arrows to indicate the flow of data (e.g., from the client → transport layer → protocol processing → server core and the reverse for responses).
   • Color Coding/Shapes: Use color or distinct shapes to differentiate between:
       – Core Logic Components (e.g., use rectangles in one color).
       – Internal Utility Layers (protocol/schema – use another color).
       – Communication Layers (Transports – use a different shape or color to signify external integration).
   • Notes or Callouts: Mark unique features such as “bidirectional communication supported by stdio and SSE” or “stateless HTTP operations” to highlight key differences.

8. Tailoring the Diagram for the mcp-golang Project:
   • For a full-stack style application like mcp-golang (which mixes server and client aspects but is fundamentally a middleware/protocol implementation), emphasize the segregation between the transport mechanism and the core protocol-driven logic.
   • Highlight the auto-generation of endpoints (for tools, prompts, resources), so include a note showing “Automatic Endpoint Generation” linked between protocol and core API.
   • Include a separate section or callout for “Extensions & Custom Transports” to document potential extension points which might be important for further integration.

By following these guidelines, the principal software engineer will create a system design diagram that is detailed, well-organized, and closely aligned with the project’s intrinsic modularity. Remember to review the docs/architecture.mdx for any additional insights that could refine this diagram further. This approach will ensure that all essential architectural elements of mcp-golang are captured clearly and accurately.
</explanation>
